aboutKids: A tiny spider climbs up a water spout. Rain washes it down, the sun comes out to dry everything, and up it climbs again.
story: No one knows who made it up. The earliest known print is a 'Spider Song' in Arthur Walbridge North's travel book Camp and Camino in Lower California (1910), with more grown-up wording. Children's versions with hand motions were printed in 1948, including in Ruth Crawford Seeger's American Folk Songs for Children.
funFact: In Britain and Australia the same little spider has a different name: Incy Wincy Spider.
myth: Online claims that the rhyme secretly has a dark meaning (for example, a warning about tipsy travellers on trains) have no credible source. It is simply a fingerplay about a determined spider.

writtenBy: Melody: Mildred J. Hill (from 'Good Morning to All', words by Patty Smith Hill). Birthday words: author unknown
year: 1893 (melody); 1912 (birthday words and melody in print together)
aboutKids: Everyone sings together to make someone feel special on their birthday, the day they were born.
story: Kentucky sisters Mildred and Patty Hill, teachers of young children, published the tune as a classroom greeting, 'Good Morning to All', in 1893. Birthday words spread by singing and were printed with the tune by 1912. A long copyright dispute ended when a US court approved a 2016 settlement declaring the song public domain.
funFact: Guinness World Records has called it the most recognized song in the English language.
myth: It is often said that Patty Hill wrote the birthday words. That has never been proven; historian Robert Brauneis says no one knows who first sang birthday words to the tune.

writtenBy: Music: Johannes Brahms. German words: Des Knaben Wunderhorn folk collection, second verse adapted from Georg Scherer. English words: traditional
aboutKids: A soft, swaying song that helps a baby close their eyes, snuggle in, and drift off to sleep.
story: Brahms wrote this Wiegenlied (cradle song) in 1868 as a gift for his friend Bertha Faber when her second son was born. The publisher Simrock issued it that November, and it was first performed publicly in Vienna in December 1869, with Clara Schumann at the piano. It soon became one of the most famous lullabies anywhere.
funFact: Brahms hid a little tune in the piano part: a Viennese song Bertha used to sing to him years earlier, when they first met.

aboutKids: Friends ride a horse-drawn sleigh across the snow, with little bells jingling and everyone laughing as they go.
story: James Lord Pierpont copyrighted the song in 1857 as 'One Horse Open Sleigh', and it was republished as Jingle Bells in 1859. It is a winter sleigh-ride song and never mentions Christmas; it became a holiday favorite later, helped by Bing Crosby and the Andrews Sisters' 1943 recording.
funFact: In December 1965, Gemini 6 astronauts played it on a tiny harmonica and bells, the first song played in space.
myth: A popular story says Pierpont wrote it for a Thanksgiving program at his father's Sunday school. This is unproven, as is Medford, Massachusetts' claim that he wrote it at a local tavern in 1850.

writtenBy: Words: Traditional English nursery rhyme. Tune: Effie I. Canning (born Effie Crockett)
aboutKids: A grown-up gently rocks a sleepy baby, swaying softly like tree branches in a breeze, until the baby falls asleep.
story: The words first appeared in Mother Goose's Melody, printed in London around 1765. The tune most people sing came much later: Effie Crockett said she made it up as a teenager in Massachusetts. Published in 1886 under the name Effie I. Canning after it was used in the play The Old Homestead, it sold strongly as sheet music.
funFact: Effie Canning said she was only about 15 when she made up the famous tune.
myth: Popular claims that the rhyme was inspired by Native American cradles hung in trees, a woman living in a Derbyshire yew tree, or a political joke about King James II are unproven guesses; the Opies record them without endorsing any.
catalogNote: Sources differ slightly on the tune's first publication: the Library of Congress says 1886 (published by Charles D. Blake), while Wikipedia says probably 1884. Blake is also sometimes credited with the tune.

writtenBy: Traditional German folk song ('Alle meine Entchen'). English words: Little Duet
aboutKids: A family of little ducks paddles across the water, dipping their heads down and lifting their tails up high.
story: Alle meine Entchen is perhaps the best-known children's song in the German-speaking world, and no one knows who wrote it. The tune appears in 18th-century dance manuscripts, one dated around 1750. The words were first printed in Wilhelm Raabe's 1859 novel, where he called it a children's rhyme.
funFact: Its tune climbs up step by step like a staircase, so it is often one of the first songs German children learn on an instrument.
catalogNote: The catalog dates the song to the 19th century; that fits the words, but the melody is older, found in manuscripts from c. 1750 and 1784. Attributions to Ernst Anschütz or Gustav Eskuche are not supported.

writtenBy: Words: August Heinrich Hoffmann von Fallersleben. Tune: traditional Austrian and Bavarian folk melody. English words: Little Duet
aboutKids: A cuckoo bird calls from the woods to tell everyone that winter is over and spring is here.
story: The poet Hoffmann von Fallersleben wrote this spring poem in 1835 and published it in 1837. In 1842 it was printed with an older folk tune known around Vienna and Bavaria since about 1817. The cuckoo words slowly replaced the old ones and became a staple of kindergartens and family singing.
funFact: Before it was about a cuckoo, the same tune was sung about a little goldfinch who was feeling poorly.
catalogNote: Catalog says 'Published 1835'; the poem was written in 1835 but first published in 1837 (without music) and first printed with this tune in 1842. Public-domain basis is unaffected.

aboutKids: Doctor Foster walks to the town of Gloucester on a rainy day and splashes right into a very big puddle.
story: The rhyme was first printed in its familiar form by James Orchard Halliwell in 1844, though a different rhyme about a Dr. Foster going to Gloucester appeared in 1810. Its author is unknown. Gloucester is a real English city, and the short, bouncy verse has been passed between parents and children ever since.
funFact: The rhyme pairs 'puddle' with 'middle', which may hint at an older word, 'piddle', meaning a small stream.
myth: A popular theory says the rhyme is about King Edward I getting stuck in mud in Gloucester and refusing to return. It was only a suggestion (Boyd Smith, 1920); there is no evidence, and the Ballad Index finds it unconvincing.

writtenBy: Music: Antonin Dvorak. English words: Little Duet
origin: Czech composer, written in the United States
aboutKids: A slow, gentle tune about the cozy feeling of going home, where the people who love you are waiting.
story: Dvorak wrote his Symphony 'From the New World' in 1893 while directing a music school in New York. It premiered at Carnegie Hall that December. In the slow Largo movement, a solo English horn plays this calm melody. Dvorak said the movement was linked to Longfellow's poem The Song of Hiawatha.
funFact: Astronaut Neil Armstrong took a tape recording of the New World Symphony with him on the Apollo 11 Moon landing mission in 1969.
myth: Many people believe the melody is an old spiritual. It is Dvorak's own tune; the song Goin' Home was created in 1922 when his former student William Arms Fisher set words to it.

aboutKids: Little Boy Blue is meant to look after the sheep and cows, but he has curled up for a nap under a haystack.
story: The rhyme was printed in London around 1744, in one of the earliest books of nursery rhymes, and is probably older. No author is known. It is most likely just what it seems: a picture of a young farm helper who should be blowing his horn to call the animals but has fallen asleep.
funFact: Shakespeare's play King Lear includes lines about a shepherd and sheep in the corn that may echo this very old rhyme.
myth: A popular claim says Little Boy Blue was Cardinal Thomas Wolsey. The idea comes from Katherine Elwes Thomas (1930); the Opies and later researchers reject it.
catalogNote: Sources agree on c. 1744 but not on the book: Wikipedia cites Tommy Thumb's Little Song Book, the Ballad Index (after Devlin) cites Nancy Cock's Song Book; I could not confirm it in Tommy Thumb's Pretty Song Book as the catalog states.

aboutKids: Lucy Locket loses her little purse, and her friend Kitty Fisher finds it. The purse was empty, except for a pretty ribbon.
story: James Orchard Halliwell recorded the rhyme in 1842, though it was already popular in Britain and America. The name Lucy Lockit appears in John Gay's The Beggar's Opera (1728). It is often sung to the tune of Yankee Doodle, and teachers use a simple three-note playground chant for it.
funFact: A pocket used to be a separate little pouch tied around the waist under a skirt, so it really could get lost.
myth: The rhyme is often said to be about two real, famous 18th-century London women who were rivals. Halliwell suggested this, but no evidence has been found that the rhyme describes real people.

writtenBy: Words: Sarah Josepha Hale. Tune: traditional American (shared with the chorus of 'Goodnight, Ladies')
aboutKids: Mary has a fluffy little lamb who loves her so much that it follows her all the way to school.
story: Sarah Josepha Hale published the poem in Poems for Our Children (Boston, 1830). Lowell Mason set it to music in the 1830s, but that tune has fallen out of use. Today it is sung to the melody of the 'Merrily we roll along' chorus, with repeated phrases added to the verses.
funFact: In 1877 Thomas Edison recited this rhyme into his new phonograph, the first words ever recorded on it.
myth: Mary Sawyer of Sterling, Massachusetts later said a young man named John Roulstone wrote the first verse after her lamb came to school. No evidence beyond her memory supports this; the earliest records support Hale as author.
catalogNote: Catalog credits the melody to Lowell Mason. His 1830s setting is no longer used; the familiar tune is the one shared with Goodnight, Ladies / Merrily We Roll Along.

writtenBy: Traditional American; linked to 'Goodnight, Ladies', whose earliest form is credited to E. P. Christy
aboutKids: Friends roll happily along together, over the hills and far away, singing as they go.
story: The song grew out of 'Goodnight, Ladies'. Its earliest form, 'Farewell, Ladies', was printed in 1847 and credited to E. P. Christy, whose touring troupe likely sang it to close their shows. The full song, including the rolling-along chorus, was first published in 1867.
funFact: Its tune is the same one most children now use to sing Mary Had a Little Lamb.
catalogNote: Catalog treats the rolling-along chorus as part of Christy's 1847 song. The 1847 print was 'Farewell, Ladies'; the chorus is first documented in the 1867 publication, after Christy's death (1862), so his authorship of that chorus is unconfirmed. Public-domain status is unaffected.

origin: England (also early in the United States)
aboutKids: A counting rhyme that goes from one to ten while a child buckles shoes, knocks on a door and picks up sticks.
story: The rhyme was first printed in Songs for the Nursery, published in London in 1805, but is probably much older. No author is known. It was made to help small children learn to count, and Victorian artist Walter Crane later illustrated it in popular picture books.
funFact: An elderly woman told a folklorist that children in Wrentham, Massachusetts used a longer version of this rhyme as early as 1780.

aboutKids: A clapping game about a pot of pea porridge. Some like it hot, some like it cold, and some like it old.
story: Its origins are unknown. The earliest known version is a riddle in John Newbery's Mother Goose's Melody, from around the 1760s. Pease porridge, now called pease pudding, is a thick dish of boiled split peas. Children pair up and clap hands, thighs and each other's palms in time with the words.
funFact: Long ago 'pease' meant the food itself, like 'oatmeal'. The words 'pea' and 'peas' came later.
catalogNote: Wikipedia dates Mother Goose's Melody c. 1760, matching this entry, but the catalog's Rock-a-bye Baby entry dates the same book c. 1765 (the Library of Congress also says c. 1765). Consider using one date for the book across the catalog.

aboutKids: A child carries a little green and yellow basket with a letter inside, then drops it on the way.
story: The rhyme was first noted in the United States in 1879 as a circle game: one child walks around the outside of the ring, drops a handkerchief behind someone, and gets chased. In 1938 Ella Fitzgerald and Al Feldman (Van Alexander) turned it into a swing hit with Chick Webb's orchestra.
funFact: Ella Fitzgerald was just 21 when her version of this playground rhyme became her first million-selling record.
catalogNote: The 1879 date rests on one secondary source (Studwell and Baldin, The Big Band Reader, 2000); I could not find the original 1879 printing.

writtenBy: Words: Septimus Winner. Tune: German folk song 'Zu Lauterbach'
aboutKids: Someone has lost their little puppy and looks everywhere, wondering where the dog could be.
story: Philadelphia songwriter Septimus Winner published 'Der Deitcher's Dog' in 1864, a comic song written in a German-American accent and set to the German folk tune 'Zu Lauterbach'. It sold very well in his lifetime, and its first verse later became a much-loved nursery song.
funFact: Winner also wrote songs as 'Alice Hawthorne', a pen name taken from his mother's family, who were related to author Nathaniel Hawthorne.

year: 1803 (first print, as 'Molly Put the Kettle On'); 1841 (modern words)
origin: England (early prints also in Dublin and New York)
aboutKids: Polly puts the kettle on so everyone can have tea, and her sister Sukey takes it off again.
story: Joseph Dale published it in London in 1803 as 'Molly Put the Kettle On', to a tune known since the 1770s. Versions with Polly were printed in Dublin and New York in the same years. Its modern words were first recorded in Charles Dickens' novel Barnaby Rudge (1841). Polly was a pet name for Mary.
funFact: In Barnaby Rudge, a talking raven named Grip calls out this rhyme. Dickens kept a real pet raven, also named Grip.
catalogNote: Catalog cites words and tune in 'A Collection of Songs' (c. 1803); the documented 1803 print is Joseph Dale's London sheet 'Molly Put the Kettle On', and I could not confirm the collection title. Barnaby Rudge (1841) gives the words only, not the tune.

aboutKids: Friends skip around in a circle, holding hands and swapping partners, laughing and dancing as they go.
story: Skip to My Lou was a play-party song from the American frontier. Where dancing to instruments was frowned upon for religious reasons, young people sang and played ring games instead. Couples skipped in a circle while one player in the middle chose a new partner. Folklorists John and Alan Lomax called it an ice-breaker.
funFact: The 'lou' in the title probably comes from the Scottish word 'loo', which means love.
catalogNote: Carl Sandburg wrote that it was a popular party game in Abraham Lincoln's Indiana youth (1810s-1820s), which would place it before the 1840s; this is anecdotal and unverified.

aboutKids: A friendly question game: do you know the muffin man who lives on Drury Lane and brings fresh muffins to the door?
story: The song was first recorded in a British manuscript around 1820, now in Oxford's Bodleian Library. Muffin men really existed: street sellers brought bread-like English muffins door to door in 19th-century London. Children have played it as a question-and-answer game, a guessing game and a ring dance.
funFact: In the Dutch version, the muffin man becomes a mussel man, and Drury Lane becomes a fishing harbour near The Hague.
myth: An internet story claims the song warned children about a dangerous baker named Frederick Thomas Lynwood. Snopes and Mental Floss found no record he existed; the tale traces to a parody website.
catalogNote: Mental Floss reports an earlier printing of the verse, with different wording, in an 1819 book; the catalog's claim that the c. 1820 manuscript includes the tune is unverified.
